entities.summary:
The State Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg, Russia is one of the world's largest and most prestigious art museums, founded in 1764 by Empress Catherine the Great. Housing over 3 million items across six interconnected buildings including the Winter Palace — former residence of Russian emperors — the Hermitage's collection spans 3 million years of human civilization and includes masterpieces by Leonardo, Rembrandt, Michelangelo, Raphael, and Van Gogh.

Catherine the Great began the collection by purchasing 225 Dutch and Flemish paintings in 1764, then systematically acquired the greatest private collections in Europe over her 34-year reign. She purchased works from Prussia, France, Britain, and other European states, building one of the finest art collections in existence by the time of her death in 1796. The Hermitage became the visible embodiment of Russia's aspiration to be recognized as a European civilization.

The museum survived the 1917 Revolution, the Siege of Leningrad (1941-1944) during which collections were evacuated to Sverdlovsk, and Soviet ideological pressures. The Hermitage complex — Winter Palace, Small Hermitage, Large Hermitage, New Hermitage, and Hermitage Theater — was built across three centuries and represents the pinnacle of European palatial architecture on Russian soil. The museum's unique character blends unparalleled imperial collections with the building that witnessed the October Revolution in 1917.
